162.title: The path of the deathless (21–23)
162.hook: earnestness is the path to the deathless; the careless are as if dead already
162.howItsDone: Buddhist teachers often stress appamada, heedfulness, and recall the Buddha's last words urging his followers to strive on with heedfulness.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the cowherd, and your line: not someone else's cows. Which verse did you live instead of reading? Day one hundred sixty-two, and chapter two begins.
screen: `OTHER PEOPLE'S COWS — NOT SOMEONE ELSE'S COWS.`

segments.voice: A car pulls into the driveway, and the driver has no memory of the drive. A bag of chips is empty by the end of the show, and only the first one was tasted. A friend gets a “yeah, totally,” and a minute later the listener has no idea what was said. Hours can pass like that. The body is there; nobody's home. Chapter two of the Dhammapada has a blunt name for that state, and a single word for its opposite. Today: the path of the deathless.
screen: `THE DRIVE YOU DON'T REMEMBER.` → `THE BODY'S THERE; NOBODY'S HOME.` → `A BLUNT NAME FOR IT.`

segments.voice: The word is appamada. It's built from pamada, which means carelessness, heedlessness, drifting, and the little prefix a-, which turns it around. So appamada is not-drifting: heedfulness, alertness, care. Müller translates it earnestness. Here's verse twenty-one in his English: “Earnestness is the path of immortality (Nirvana), thoughtlessness the path of death. Those who are in earnest do not die, those who are thoughtless are as if dead already.” As if dead already. That's the blunt name. Not a threat about the future, but a description of the drive you don't remember. The word Müller renders immortality is amata, the deathless, one of the old names for nibbana. Verses twenty-two and twenty-three go on: the wise, who understand this, delight in heedfulness, and by steady, strong practice they reach nibbana, the highest happiness. This one word matters so much that the tradition remembers it at the very end of the Buddha's life. In the long discourse on his final days, his last words to the monks, in Rhys Davids' translation, are: “Decay is inherent in all component things! Work out your salvation with diligence!” That last word, diligence, translates the same word: appamada. Some teachers say the whole teaching, at the end, is folded into it. Notice it doesn't mean rushing or straining. The heedful person isn't frantic. They're simply here: tasting the chip, hearing the friend, seeing the road. And the verse's claim is striking. In its terms, that kind of presence isn't only the path to something later. The heedful are the ones who are alive.
screen: `APPAMADA — NOT DRIFTING.` · `THE CARELESS: AS IF DEAD ALREADY.` · `AMATA, THE DEATHLESS.` · `THE BUDDHA'S LAST WORD.` · then, large: `HEEDFUL IS ALIVE.`

segments.voice: Let's practice appamada with the simplest task there is: breathing. Sit, and give this breath your full attention, from the first touch of air to the last. Then the next. When you notice you've drifted, and you will, that noticing is the moment of heedfulness. It isn't a failure; it's the practice. Come back, without scolding. Later today, choose one ordinary task: brushing your teeth, washing a mug, tying your shoes, and do it with the same full attention. The bell holds the time.
Appamada. Heedfulness: the opposite of drifting. The path to the deathless, and the Buddha's last word.
Your line: heedful is alive. Today, do one task with full attention, start to finish, and notice how different it feels from doing it on autopilot. Day one hundred sixty-two.

it means not drifting: simply being present and careful, not frantic.
the Buddha's last words, in Rhys Davids' translation, end 'work out your salvation with diligence'
diligence there translates appamada, the same word as chapter two.
'as if dead already' is a threat about what happens after death
it describes the state of drifting through life with nobody home.

fork.setup: you notice, halfway through the sit, that your mind has been planning dinner for a minute. what does heedfulness look like now?
options: scold yourself and start over.
notice it and come back to the breath.
give up on the sit.
fork.reveal: the noticing itself is appamada. coming back, without scolding, is the practice.

original.note: Pali: heedfulness, from a- (not) and pamada (carelessness).

trapdoor: what you thought: 'earnestness' means being very serious.
what it means: appamada is not drifting: full attention, the opposite of autopilot.

163.title: An island (24–28)
163.hook: by effort and restraint the wise make an island no flood can overwhelm
163.howItsDone: Buddhist teachers often use the island verse to describe steady daily practice as a refuge, and the story of Culapanthaka and the white cloth is a favorite example of awakening through one simple, repeated practice.

segments.voice: Yesterday, appamada, heedfulness, and your line: heedful is alive. Which task did you do with full attention? Day one hundred sixty-three.

In the Ganges plain, the monsoon floods can spread for miles. Fields vanish. Roads vanish. From above, the land is a sheet of brown water. But here and there you see them: small patches of raised ground where a village has built up the earth, year after year, basket by basket, so that when the water rises, there's still somewhere dry to stand. Nobody builds that in one season. And nobody builds it during the flood. Today, verses twenty-four to twenty-eight: an island.
screen: `THE MONSOON FLOOD.` → `RAISED GROUND, BASKET BY BASKET.` → `NOT BUILT DURING THE FLOOD.`

segments.voice: Verse twenty-five, in Müller's English: “By rousing himself, by earnestness, by restraint and control, the wise man may make for himself an island which no flood can overwhelm.” Four tools: rousing yourself, heedfulness, restraint and self-control. And one result: an island. In the Buddha's teaching, the flood is a standing image for the currents that sweep people along: craving, views, ignorance, the endless round. You can't stop the river. You can raise the ground you stand on. The word for island is dipa. And here's a lovely puzzle: in Pali, dipa can mean island, and it can also mean lamp. When the Buddha, near the end of his life, told his followers to be a dipa for themselves, translators split. Rhys Davids gave lamps. Many modern translators give islands. The tradition has lived with both. The commentary tells verse twenty-five about a monk called Little Panthaka. For four months he couldn't memorize a single verse; it slipped away as soon as he learned the next line. His brother, also a monk, told him to give up and go home. The Buddha found him crying outside the monastery, handed him a clean white cloth, and told him to rub it while repeating a simple phrase about removing dirt. As he rubbed, the cloth grew grimy in his hand, and he saw, in that small change, how everything changes. The story says he awakened right there. The verses around it add that fools give themselves to carelessness, while the wise guard heedfulness like their best treasure. No one built Panthaka's island with scholarship. He built it with one small practice, repeated.
screen: `FOUR TOOLS, ONE ISLAND.` · `THE FLOOD: WHAT SWEEPS US ALONG.` · `DIPA — ISLAND, OR LAMP.` · `LITTLE PANTHAKA AND THE WHITE CLOTH.` · then, large: `MAKE AN ISLAND.`

segments.voice: Sit and settle. Think of the flood in your own life: the busiest week, the hard news, the tired evening when everything slides. Now ask: what small thing, done every day, would give me somewhere dry to stand? Maybe it's this sit. Maybe three breaths before opening email. Maybe a walk after dinner. Choose one small habit, small enough that you could keep it even on a bad day. Picture yourself doing it tomorrow, then the next day. One basket of earth at a time. Then rest with the breath. The bell holds the time.
An island. The raised ground the wise build, by effort and restraint, so that no flood can overwhelm them.
Your line: make an island. Today, begin the small daily habit you chose, and do it once, even if it takes one minute. Day one hundred sixty-three.

fork.reveal: the Buddha found him, gave him a clean cloth and a phrase about removing dirt. watching the cloth grow grimy, he saw how everything changes.

original.note: Pali: island, and also lamp: the word behind 'make an island.'

trapdoor: what you thought: the island means cutting yourself off from other people.
what it means: raised ground, built by steady effort, where you can stand when the flood comes.
what a scholar hears: Pali dipa covers Sanskrit dvipa (island) and dipa (lamp); translators of 'attadipa' in DN 16 have split between 'lamp' and 'island.'

164.title: The racehorse (29–32)
164.hook: awake among the sleeping, the wise move on like a racehorse leaving a nag behind
164.howItsDone: Some Buddhist monasteries rise well before dawn for sitting and chanting, and some lay practitioners keep a short sitting early in the morning before the household wakes.

segments.voice: Yesterday, an island, and your line: make an island. Did you start your small daily habit, even for a minute? Day one hundred sixty-four, the last day of chapter two.

There's a particular quiet at five in the morning. The house is asleep. The street is asleep. Even the phone is quiet, because everyone who might send a message is asleep too. People up at that hour, for a flight or a baby or a shift, sometimes call it a secret extra room in the day. In some monasteries the bell rings in that room, well before dawn, for sitting and chanting while the town sleeps. The Dhammapada has a picture for someone awake while others sleep. Today, verses twenty-nine to thirty-two: the racehorse.
screen: `FIVE IN THE MORNING.` → `A SECRET EXTRA ROOM.` → `THE MONASTERY IS ALREADY UP.`

segments.voice: Verse twenty-nine, in Müller's English: “Earnest among the thoughtless, awake among the sleepers, the wise man advances like a racer, leaving behind the hack.” A racer and a hack: a fast racehorse and a tired old nag. The commentary tells it about two monks who went to the forest together for the rains. One gathered firewood, sat by the fire in the evenings, and chatted with the young novices half the night. The other kept to his practice, sitting and walking, and slept only in the middle watch. By the end of the rains the second had awakened. When they came back, the chatty monk told the Buddha his friend had been lazy. The Buddha said it was the other way around, and spoke the verse. The friend by the fire was the nag. It's worth being careful here. The verse isn't praising people who sleep four hours and brag about it. Awake in the Dhammapada mostly means inwardly awake: heedful, present, not drifting. The two monks were in the same forest, with the same hours. One spent them drifting; one spent them awake. The chapter closes with three more verses. Heedfulness, it says, raised the god Indra to lordship among the gods. The heedful monk moves like a fire, burning up his fetters, small and large. And someone who delights in heedfulness can't fall away; they're close to nibbana. So look back at chapter two: the path of the deathless, an island, and now the racehorse. One word, heedfulness, seen three ways.
screen: `A RACER AND A HACK.` · `TWO MONKS, ONE FOREST.` · `AWAKE MEANS INWARDLY AWAKE.` · `HEEDFULNESS, SEEN THREE WAYS.` · then, large: `AWAKE AMONG THE SLEEPING.`

segments.voice: Sit, and imagine the house very early, before anyone is up. No messages, no noise. Just you, the dark window, maybe the first birds. Let that stillness be here now, even if it's the middle of the afternoon. Feel what it's like to be awake while the world is quiet: the breath, the body, the room. Then, if it fits your life, think about tomorrow. Could you get up ten or fifteen minutes earlier, just once, and sit in that extra room? Only if it helps, not if it costs you sleep you need. The bell holds the time.
The racehorse. The heedful one, awake among the sleepers, moving on like a racer leaving the tired horse behind.
Your line: awake among the sleeping. Tomorrow, if you can, get up a little early once and spend those minutes awake, not scrolling. Day one hundred sixty-four.

165.title: The fletcher (33–34)
165.hook: the wise straighten the trembling mind as a fletcher straightens an arrow; the mind flaps like a fish on dry land
165.howItsDone: Buddhist meditation teachers often use the fletcher image to describe training the mind patiently, and the chapter on citta is taught as a guide to working with the mind.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the racehorse, and your line: awake among the sleeping. Did you find a few quiet minutes before the house woke? Day one hundred sixty-five, and chapter three: thought.

Before factories, arrows were made by hand, one at a time, by a craftsman called a fletcher. The hard part wasn't the feathers or the point. It was the shaft. A length of cane or wood is never quite straight. So the fletcher would warm it gently over a fire, then sight down its length, find the bend, and ease it true, a little at a time, between his hands or in a notched tool. Then sight again. Then ease again. Patient, careful, never snapping it. The Dhammapada says that's exactly what the wise do with something else. Today, verses thirty-three and thirty-four: the fletcher.
screen: `A FLETCHER AT HIS FIRE.` → `SIGHT DOWN THE SHAFT.` → `EASE THE BEND, NEVER SNAP IT.`

segments.voice: Chapter three is called citta, which Müller translates thought. Citta is one of the Pali words for mind: the heart-mind that thinks, feels and wants, all at once. Verse thirty-three: “As a fletcher makes straight his arrow, a wise man makes straight his trembling and unsteady thought, which is difficult to guard, difficult to hold back.” Trembling and unsteady. That's the mind the verse starts with: not a calm mind that needs a little polish, but one that shakes. Verse thirty-four gives the picture: “As a fish taken from his watery home and thrown on the dry ground, our thought trembles all over.” Anyone who's watched a fish on a dock knows that flapping: frantic, desperate, going nowhere. That's the mind when it's pulled out of its old habits: it wants to jump back in. The commentary tells these verses about Meghiya, a monk who was attending the Buddha. He saw a beautiful mango grove and asked to go and meditate there. The Buddha asked him to wait. He asked again, and again, and finally the Buddha let him go. In the grove, Meghiya's mind was flooded with thoughts of desire, anger and harm, and he came back shaken. His mind had flapped like the fish. So the verses don't pretend this is easy. They name the difficulty, and then they give a craft. Not force. The fletcher never snaps the shaft. Warmth, patience, sight down the length, find the bend, ease it true, and sight again. That's also a fair description of the sitting you've been doing for months.
screen: `CITTA — THE HEART-MIND.` · `TREMBLING AND UNSTEADY.` · `A FISH ON DRY GROUND.` · `MEGHIYA IN THE MANGO GROVE.` · then, large: `STRAIGHTEN THE ARROW.`

segments.voice: Sit, and let the breath be the fire that warms the shaft. Now sight down the mind. What's bent in it right now? A worry leaning one way, an irritation pulling another, a plan that won't let go. Pick one bent thought. Don't wrench it. Just see it clearly, and let the next breath ease it a little: less tight, less urgent, closer to true. If it springs back, that's normal. Sight again, ease again. The bell holds the time.
Citta. The mind, or heart-mind: trembling and unsteady at first, and made straight by patient work, like an arrow.
Your line: straighten the arrow. Today, when one thought starts to bend your day, sight down it once and ease it, gently, without snapping. Day one hundred sixty-five.

trapdoor: what you thought: a wise person has a naturally steady mind.

what a scholar hears: the suttas use citta, mano and vinnana for mind, often nearly interchangeably; the Meghiya episode is also told in the Udana (4.1).

166.title: Guard the mind (35–39)
166.hook: hard to see, subtle, going where it likes: a guarded mind brings happiness
166.howItsDone: Buddhist teachers sometimes sum up the discipline as guarding the mind, and meditators practice noting where attention wanders and gently returning it.

segments.voice: Yesterday, citta, the trembling mind, and your line: straighten the arrow. Did you ease one bent thought? Day one hundred sixty-six.

A young man has just become a monk. He's sincere. Then his teachers start on the rules: how to wear the robe, how to eat, how to walk into a village, what is allowed, what is not. Rule after rule. His heart sinks. He can't possibly keep all that. Maybe he should go back to lay life after all. He's brought to the Buddha, ready to give up. And the Buddha asks him a surprisingly simple question: could you guard just one thing? Today, verses thirty-five to thirty-nine: guard the mind.
screen: `RULE AFTER RULE.` → `HIS HEART SINKS.` → `COULD YOU GUARD JUST ONE THING?`

segments.voice: In the commentary's story, the young man says yes, he could guard one thing. Then guard your mind, the Buddha says, and you won't need to worry about the rest. And he speaks verse thirty-six. Müller's English describes thoughts as “difficult to perceive, very artful,” rushing wherever they like, and it ends: “thoughts well guarded bring happiness.” Verse thirty-five says the same with a different verb: the mind is hard to hold and flighty, and “a tamed mind brings happiness.” Look at how the mind is described. Hard to see. Subtle. Going wherever it wants. Verse thirty-seven adds that it travels far, moves alone, has no body, and hides in the cave of the heart. That's not an insult. It's an honest field guide. You can't guard something you haven't looked at. Guarding here doesn't mean locking the mind in a box, or fighting every thought. The Pali word is closer to protecting, keeping watch over, the way a gatekeeper watches who comes in. Thoughts will come. The guard notices them at the gate. This one can come in. That one, the old resentment, the spiral of worry, maybe not today. Verses thirty-eight and thirty-nine finish the chapter's middle: wisdom can't grow in a mind that's always unsteady, and the one whose mind is watched and calm has nothing to fear. There's a real kindness in the story. The young man's problem wasn't lack of goodness. It was overwhelm. And the answer wasn't a longer list. It was one thing, done well: watch the gate.
screen: `JUST ONE THING TO GUARD.` · `HARD TO SEE, GOING WHERE IT LIKES.` · `A GATEKEEPER, NOT A PRISON.` · `WISDOM NEEDS A STEADY MIND.` · then, large: `GUARD THE MIND.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably and become a gatekeeper. The breath is your post. From here, just watch where the mind goes. Off to a memory. Off to a plan. Off to a song. Each time, notice where it went, name it softly, “planning,” “remembering,” and come back to the post. You're not trying to stop it from going. You're learning its routes, the places it likes to wander. By the end, you may know a few of them by heart. The bell holds the time.
Rakkhetha. Let one guard: the mind, hard to see, subtle, going where it likes, watched like a gate, brings happiness when guarded.
Your line: watch the gate. Today, notice three places your mind wanders to without asking, and watch the gate for the one that costs you most. Day one hundred sixty-six.

screen: `DAY 166 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THE BODY LIKE A JAR.`

167.title: The body like a jar (40–43)
167.hook: the body is fragile as a jar; a well-directed mind does more good than mother or father (Dhammapada 43)
167.howItsDone: Buddhists often reflect on the body's fragility as a way of loosening attachment, and the story of the Buddha washing the sick monk Tissa is told as a model of caring for the ill.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the gatekeeper, and your line: watch the gate. Where did your mind wander without asking? Day one hundred sixty-seven, the end of chapter three.

A clay water jar comes back from the well, full. Two things are true of it. It's useful every single day. And one slip on a wet step, one knock against a doorframe, and it's gone. That doesn't make the jar worthless. It just means carrying it with care, both hands, eyes on the step. The Dhammapada holds the human body up beside that jar. Today, verses forty to forty-three: the body like a jar.
screen: `A CLAY JAR FROM THE WELL.` → `USEFUL EVERY DAY.` → `ONE SLIP, AND IT'S GONE.`

segments.voice: Verse forty says: knowing the body is fragile like a jar, make the mind firm like a fortress, and meet Mara with the weapon of wisdom. Fragile body, firm mind. Then verse forty-one, a stark one: “Before long, alas! this body will lie on the earth, despised, without understanding, like a useless log.” The commentary sets that verse in a moving scene. A monk named Tissa fell ill with sores that covered his whole body. His robes stuck to him. The other monks couldn't bear it and left him alone. The Buddha, seeing this, heated water himself, washed the sick monk with his own hands, and washed his robe and dried it in the sun. Then, while Tissa lay clean and comfortable, he spoke the verse. So the verse about the log isn't contempt for the body. It comes from the one person who was willing to wash it. The body is fragile, and it deserves care. It just isn't the whole story. Then the chapter turns. Verse forty-two says a wrongly directed mind does us more harm than any enemy. And verse forty-three is its bright twin: “Not a mother, not a father will do so much, nor any other relative; a well-directed mind will do us greater service.” That's a big claim. A good mother feeds, worries, teaches. The verse says your own mind, pointed well, can do even more, because it goes everywhere with you. So chapter three closes where it began: straighten the arrow, guard the gate, and carry the jar with care.
screen: `FRAGILE BODY, FIRM MIND.` · `LIKE A USELESS LOG.` · `THE BUDDHA WASHES THE SICK MONK.` · `BETTER THAN MOTHER OR FATHER.` · then, large: `MORE THAN A MOTHER CAN.`

segments.voice: If there's a cup or a mug near you, pick it up and hold it in both hands. If not, just imagine one. Feel its weight, its smoothness, its edge. Know that it can break. Not to be grim. Just to see it clearly. Now feel your own hands holding it, the same way: warm, useful, fragile. Set the cup down gently. Then sit with the breath, and let the mind be firm and kind, like someone who knows how to carry a jar. The bell holds the time.
The body like a jar. Fragile, useful, and worth carrying with care, while the mind, pointed well, does more good than a mother or father.
screen: `THE BODY LIKE A JAR — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: more than a mother can. Today, point your mind somewhere kind once, the way a good parent would point you. Day one hundred sixty-seven.

trapdoor: what you thought: the Dhammapada teaches disgust for the body.
what it means: the body is fragile and deserves care; it just isn't the whole story.

168.title: The garland-maker (44–48)
168.hook: who will pick the well-taught path as a skilled hand picks flowers; death carries off the one still gathering
168.howItsDone: Flower garlands are among the most common Buddhist offerings, and teachers use the chapter on flowers to encourage choosing one teaching to practice rather than collecting many.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the body like a jar, and your line: more than a mother can. Where did you point your mind kindly? Day one hundred sixty-eight, the end of the week, and chapter four: flowers.
screen: `THE BODY LIKE A JAR — MORE THAN A MOTHER CAN.`

segments.voice: Walk past a temple in India, Sri Lanka or Thailand early in the morning and you'll see them: the garland-makers. They sit with baskets of jasmine, marigold, lotus, and their hands move fast, choosing, threading, knotting. They don't take every flower. A skilled one can tell at a glance which bloom is fresh, which will last the day, which is already turning. Choosing well is the whole craft. The fourth chapter of the Dhammapada opens at that basket. Today, verses forty-four to forty-eight: the garland-maker.
screen: `BASKETS OF JASMINE AND MARIGOLD.` → `HANDS CHOOSING, THREADING.` → `CHOOSING WELL IS THE CRAFT.`

segments.voice: The commentary says a group of monks, back from a journey, sat talking about the ground they'd walked over: level here, muddy there, stony, rough. The Buddha told them: that's the earth outside. Look at the earth inside you. And he spoke the chapter's first two verses. Who will master this earth, he asks, and the realms beyond it? Who will pick out the well-taught path of the dhamma, the way a skilled garland-maker picks out the right flower? And the answer: the one in training will. Not the one with the most flowers, but the one who can choose. Verse forty-six adds that the body is like foam, like a mirage. Then verse forty-seven, with a hard image: “Death carries off a man who is gathering flowers and whose mind is distracted, as a flood carries off a sleeping village.” Gathering flowers, here, means collecting pleasures, one after another, never finished, never quite satisfied. Verse forty-eight says death takes that person “before he is satiated”, still reaching for the next bloom. Put the two pictures side by side. One person gathers endlessly and never makes a garland. The other chooses carefully and makes something. Look back at this week and you'll see you've been gathering well: appamada, heedfulness. An island. The racehorse, awake among the sleepers. Citta and the fletcher. The gatekeeper. The jar. That's a lot of flowers. The garland-maker's question is simpler: which one will you actually pick up and use today?
screen: `THE EARTH OUTSIDE, THE EARTH INSIDE.` · `PICK THE PATH LIKE THE RIGHT FLOWER.` · `THE ONE STILL GATHERING.` · `THIS WEEK'S BASKET.` · then, large: `PICK THE FLOWER.`

segments.voice: Sit and breathe, and picture the week's teachings laid out in a basket in front of you. Heedful is alive. Make an island. Awake among the sleeping. Straighten the arrow. Guard the mind. More than a mother can. Look them over like a garland-maker: which is fresh for you today? Which fits the day you're about to have? Pick one. Just one. Hold it, and let the others rest in the basket. Then sit quietly with the one you chose. The bell holds the time.
The garland-maker. The skilled one who chooses the right flower from the basket, as the wise pick out the well-taught path.
Your line: pick the flower. Today, use the one teaching you chose, once, on purpose, and let the rest wait. Day one hundred sixty-eight.

match.prompt: match the pictures in verses forty-four to forty-eight.

myth: the garland-maker verse praises collecting as many flowers as possible
it praises choosing well: picking out the right flower, the well-taught path.
in the commentary, the monks had been talking about the roads they'd walked
the Buddha turned them from the earth outside to the earth inside.
verse forty-six compares the body to foam and a mirage
both look solid and aren't.

fork.setup: you've just come back from a long walk with your friends, and you're all comparing notes on the road: muddy here, rocky there. the Buddha joins you. what does he say?
options: tell me which road was best.
that's the earth outside; look at the earth inside.
you should have taken a cart.
fork.reveal: in the commentary he turns their talk inward and speaks the first verses of the flower chapter.

original.note: Pali: flower, the title of chapter four (Puppha Vagga).

trapdoor: what you thought: 'gathering flowers' in verse forty-seven is a sweet, innocent picture.
what it means: it's collecting pleasures endlessly, never satisfied, and death arrives mid-gathering.
what a scholar hears: verses 44–45 turn on 'dhammapadam sudesitam' and 'kusalo pupphamiva pacessati': the well-taught dhammapada, picked as a skilled one picks a flower.

sources.ref: Dhammapada 44–46; Dhammapada-atthakatha, story of the monks talking about the earth (verses 44–45)
